reference_prompt: Original full-body creature reference for Tetherbound: Stormursa, a powerful adult storm bear evolved from Staticub. Study the installed Staticub reference/body first and preserve its face, rounded ears, muzzle and recognizable electric markings. A massive believable quadruped bear with broad shoulders, thick neck, broad planted paws, short tail, clear leg separations, and a friendly but formidable intelligent expression. Stormwood identity: muted slate-violet fur, warm copper horn-like shoulder ridges, restrained translucent glass accents and small white-violet lightning seams. Natural fur masses and readable anatomy, tactile stylized materials with the appeal of a high-quality creature adventure game, original design, no copied comparison-game characters, no Team Tether red, no clothes, no mechanical armor. Neutral balanced standing pose, mouth closed, claws visible, all four feet visible and separable, no VFX obscuring anatomy. Plain neutral light-gray background, even studio illumination, clean 3/4 view suitable for image-to-3D, no lettering, no logo, no trainer, no contact shadows painted into texture. Include separate front and side orthographic references if needed for rig assessment. Target withers height 4.10 meters, measurably larger than installed Staticub at 3.25 meters; do not shrink Staticub or existing larger creatures.

scale.rule: Final mesh bounds and in-engine posture must clear BOTH source and trainer, grow smaller side on repair. These values are targets, not measured evidence.

meshy_prompt: Use only the inspected original Stormursa reference. Preserve bear anatomy, broad shoulder silhouette, four separate articulated legs and toes, short tail, broad paws, rounded ears, visible face, slate-violet/copper/glass palette. Game-ready closed connected surface with clean deforming joints, separate muzzle/neck/paw articulation and UV textures. No baked lightning haze, no floating decorative shells, no fused front legs or occluded underbelly. Record actual settings and every task ID.
